newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore PM says his future riding on vote.
newsitem.headline: Singapore PM says his future riding on vote.

text.p: Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said on Wednesday his position and Singapore's stability could be questioned if his party fared badly in Thursday polls, even though it already has won continued control of the government.
The ruling People's Action Party (PAP) is guaranteed a majority after the January 2 election because 47 of the parliament's 83 seats are not being contested by the opposition.
But on the hustings for the remaining 36 seats, Goh made it clear strong support in the contested areas was crucial to his government's credibility.
"This election is watched not just by Singaporeans but also by foreigners, by other countries," Goh told reporters at a news conference on the campaign trail.

He said if he did not do well, foreigners would conclude his position had weakened, "which means they would say after me, who will be the next prime minister ... would I be challenged internally within the PAP, would I be challenged by others outside the PAP?
"So they would speculate as to the stability of Singapore."
The PAP has been in power since independence in 1965 and faced no opposition members in parliament until 1981. In the outgoing parliament opposition parties hold just four seats.
With that history, an increase of even a few more seats for the opposition could be seen as a major blow to the PAP and to Goh's leadership of the island-state, political analysts said.
The election has seen the introduction of additional winner-take-all, multi-member constituencies, in which the victorious party could have up to six candidates elected.
A win in a multi-member constituency could sharply increase opposition representation in parliament and that could jeopardise Goh's premiership, according to some analysts.
One such group representation constituency, where the race is believed to be close, is Cheng San, with five seats at stake.

Goh said "this battle in Cheng San is a very important battle because people will conclude, is Singapore moving closer towards a Chinese-dominant society less tolerant of other languages, religion or culture?"
The PAP has launched an all-out assault on one Workers' Party (WP) candidate in the constituency, Tang Liang Hong.
PAP leaders have accused Tang of harbouring anti-Christian and communal Chinese views in a society that witnessed racial riots in the 1960s.

State television quoted a lawyer for Goh as saying Tang had failed to respond by the deadline set out in a letter demanding he promise to apologise at a party rally and on the front page of the Straits Times newspaper on Thursday.
The lawyer's letter had said Goh would sue Tang for defamation over remarks made in an interview with the newspaper unless he met the demands by 6 p.m. (1000 GMT).
PAP leaders have not hesitated to take legal action against opposition figures in the past when they feel it is justified.

While campaigning on Wednesday, Low Thia Khiang, a Worker's Party leader, said the legal threat against Tang showed opposition parties and candidates face a great risk and pay a high price when they seek election, state television reported.

In a speech on Tuesday, Goh made it clear supporting the opposition could hit voters where they live. He said the PAP would monitor results from every voting ward, which contain about 5,000 voters each, to pinpoint the precincts that supported them and the level of that support.
Using this information Goh said the government would determine which areas, even within individual constituencies, get priority for much sought after upgrading of their housing.
